name: Maypop

knowledgeLevels.1: Maypop. Ornate purple flowers, egg-sized fruit that ripens wrinkled and yellow.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: ripe fruit only (wrinkled, yellow, fragrant). Unripe = bitter and nauseating.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: sweet-tart pulp, eaten fresh. Leaves make a mild calming tea.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: wait for the fruit to fall or wrinkle fully. One vine can feed you for a week in season.

preparation: Eat only fully ripe (wrinkled yellow) fruit. Unripe fruit will punish you.
description: a vine with elaborate purple-and-white flowers and egg-sized green fruit that wrinkles yellow when ripe
lookalikeNote: The fringed purple-white flower is unmistakable. Only the wrinkled yellow fruit is food.
codex: The Southeast's passionfruit. Ugly flower, alien fruit, honest sugar.
sources: Field validation pending — conservative well-known species

uses.note: ripe wrinkled fruit — sweet-tart pulp
leaf tea, mild and calming

name: Wild Black Cherry

knowledgeLevels.1: Wild black cherry. Tall tree, hanging clusters of small dark fruit.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: ripe fruit (dark purple-black). SPIT THE PITS — they contain cyanide compounds.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: sweet-tart fruit fresh or dried. Wilted leaves are dangerous to livestock.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: pick fully dark fruit; one tree can fill a pack. Dry cherries for winter.

preparation: Eat ripe fruit raw. Always spit the pits. Never chew them.
description: a tall tree with dark peeling bark and long hanging clusters of small dark cherries
lookalikeNote: Ripe = dark purple-black and sweet-tart. Red fruit isn't ready. Pits and wilted leaves are toxic.
codex: Cherry trees rain fruit in June. Eat the fruit, spit the pits — the rule is the recipe.
sources: Field validation pending — conservative well-known species

uses.note: ripe dark cherries — spit the pits
fallen fruit baits traps well

name: Serviceberry

knowledgeLevels.1: Serviceberry. White spring flowers, clusters of red-purple berries in June.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: ripe berries (purple, soft). Seeds contain cyanide compounds like apple seeds — don't chew masses of them.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: blueberry-almond flavor, eaten fresh or dried. Early summer staple.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: June harvest; berries ripen unevenly — pick the dark ones, leave the red. Dry for winter stores.

preparation: Eat raw when fully purple. Don't chew large quantities of seeds.
description: a small tree with white starry flowers in spring and clusters of red-to-purple berries in early summer
lookalikeNote: Ripe = purple-black and soft. Don't gorge on the seeds (cyanide compounds, like apple seeds).
codex: June's gift. Tastes like blueberry met almond. The birds know the date before you do.
sources: Field validation pending — conservative well-known species

uses.note: sweet early-summer berries

name: Groundnut

knowledgeLevels.1: Groundnut. Twining vine in wet ground; dig for strings of round tubers.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the tubers. Cook well — raw causes stomach trouble. Exceptional protein.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: more protein than any tuber you know — the staple that fed whole villages.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: dig in fall along creek banks. Boil or roast thoroughly. Leave some tubers to regrow.

preparation: Dig tubers in fall. Cook thoroughly — never eat raw.
description: a twining vine in wet ground with brownish pea-flowers and strings of round tubers underground
lookalikeNote: Twining vine with compound leaves in wet soil = groundnut. Tubers grow in a string from the vine base.
codex: The Indian potato. Protein like a tuber shouldn't have. Cook it like you mean it.
sources: Field validation pending — conservative well-known species

uses.note: protein-rich tubers — cook thoroughly

name: American Ginseng

knowledgeLevels.1: Ginseng. Whorled compound leaves, red berry cluster. You've only read about this.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the slow-grown root. Harvesting wild roots is restricted in many states — it was poached near extinction.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: traditional adaptogen and tonic. The System notes it with interest; the forest keeps it rare.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: you don't forage this. You learn it, respect it, and leave it. The knowledge is the harvest.

preparation: Not foraged. Traditional use is dried root tea — in tiny amounts, from cultivated sources only.
description: a low woodland plant with a whorl of compound leaves and a small cluster of red berries — rare, and protected
lookalikeNote: Virginia creeper seedlings and young hickory sprouts fool beginners. Ginseng's leaf whorl is distinctive — and it isn't yours to dig.
codex: Worth more than gold, rarer than honesty. The forest keeps its ginseng; so do you.
sources: Field validation pending — conservative well-known species

uses.note: traditional tonic — cultivated only, never wild-harvested

name: Wild Ginger

knowledgeLevels.1: Wild ginger. Heart-shaped leaves flat on the forest floor. You've only read about this.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the rhizome smells exactly like ginger — but it isn't. Contains aristolochic acid: toxic to kidneys.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: none safe in quantity. The System logged it as 'spice-adjacent, do not ingest'. Smell it, enjoy it, leave it.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: knowing what NOT to eat is the highest level. The scent is the lesson.

preparation: Do not use as food. Historical spice use is discontinued for good reason (kidney toxicity).
description: low heart-shaped leaves hugging the forest floor, hiding small jug-shaped flowers at the base
lookalikeNote: Heart-shaped leaves with hidden jug flowers at the base. Gingery smell with NO culinary safety — leave it alone.
codex: Smells like ginger, acts like poison. The forest's reminder that smell is not a safety test.
sources: Field validation pending — conservative well-known species

uses.note: historical use only — aristolochic acid, toxic; do not ingest

name: Prickly Pear

knowledgeLevels.1: Prickly pear. Flat pads, sharp spines. The fruits are called tunas.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: pads (nopal — vegetable), fruits (tuna — sweet). Burn off spines first or use tongs.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: pads are food AND water — chew for moisture. Fruits are high in sugar.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: singe spines over fire, then peel. Pads keep for days. In the desert, this plant is life.

preparation: Burn or scrape off glochids (tiny spines). Pads: grill or boil. Fruits: peel and eat.
description: flat paddle-shaped cactus pads, wicked spines, red-purple fruits
codex: Desert grocery store. Food, water, and medicine in one spiny package.

name: Mesquite

knowledgeLevels.1: Mesquite. Thorny tree, long bean pods. Desert staple.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: pods (sweet, grindable into flour), wood (best firewood in the desert).
knowledgeLevels.3: Mesquite flour is protein-rich and sweet. Pods can be eaten raw when ripe.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: harvest pods when dry and tan. Grind between stones. The wood burns hot and long — worth the thorns.

preparation: Pods: eat raw when ripe, or dry and grind into flour. Wood: best desert fuel.
description: thorny spreading tree, long tan bean pods, feathery leaves
codex: The desert's bread tree. Pods are candy and flour; wood is the finest fuel.

name: Salmonberry

knowledgeLevels.1: Salmonberry. Pink-orange berries, thorny canes. First berry of spring.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: berries (eat fresh), young shoots (peel and eat like asparagus).
knowledgeLevels.3: They're watery — good for hydration, not calories. Eat by the handful while working.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: follow the salmonberry bloom — it marks the start of foraging season. Shoots are best before they leaf out.

preparation: Eat berries fresh. Peel young shoots and eat raw or steamed.
description: tall thorny canes, magenta flowers, salmon-colored raspberry-like berries
codex: Spring's first gift. Not calorie-dense, but they tell you the forest is waking up.

name: Huckleberry

knowledgeLevels.1: Huckleberry. Small dark berries, mountain slopes. Bears love them.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: berries only. Richer than blueberries, harder to find.
knowledgeLevels.3: Where huckleberries grow, bears feed. Pick noisily and in groups.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: they fruit heavily every 2-3 years. Remember the good patches — they're worth defending.

preparation: Eat fresh or dry for winter. Excellent dried.
description: low shrubs, small dark-purple berries, mountain slopes and clearings
codex: The mountain's candy. Worth the climb, worth watching for bears.

name: Yaupon Holly

knowledgeLevels.1: Yaupon holly. Evergreen shrub, red berries. The leaves make tea.
knowledgeLevels.2: It's the only native North American caffeine plant. Roast the leaves, steep like tea.
knowledgeLevels.3: The 'vomitoria' name is from ceremonial overuse — normal tea won't hurt you. Don't eat the berries.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: roast leaves dark for best flavor. This is coffee when there's no coffee. Trade-worthy.

preparation: Roast leaves in a pan until dark, then steep in hot water. Do NOT eat berries.
description: evergreen shrub, small red berries, oval leaves
codex: North America's only native caffeine. The bayou's coffee.

name: Saw Palmetto

knowledgeLevels.1: Saw palmetto. Fan palms with saw-tooth stems. Blue-black berries.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: berries (edible, peppery-sweet), heart of palm (the growing tip — kills the plant).
knowledgeLevels.3: Berries are calorie-dense for their size. The saw teeth will cut you — harvest carefully.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: berries ripen in fall. Dry them for winter. Don't take the heart unless you're starving — it kills the plant.

preparation: Berries: eat raw or dried. Heart of palm: only in emergency (kills plant).
description: low fan palms, serrated stems, clusters of blue-black berries
codex: Florida's pantry palm. Berries feed you; the saw teeth remind you to be careful.

name: Sugar Maple

knowledgeLevels.1: Sugar maple. The sap makes syrup. Bark is grey, leaves turn brilliant in fall.
knowledgeLevels.2: Tap in late winter — when days thaw and nights freeze. Drill, spile, bucket.
knowledgeLevels.3: 40 gallons of sap = 1 gallon of syrup. Boil it down. It's work, but it's sugar.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: tap trees 10+ inches diameter, one tap each. The run lasts 4-6 weeks. Syrup keeps indefinitely.

preparation: Tap in late winter. Boil sap down 40:1 for syrup. Can also just drink the sap (slightly sweet water).
description: tall tree, grey bark, five-lobed leaves that flame orange in fall
codex: Liquid gold from a tree. The northeast's answer to sugar cane.
The forest's butter. Small nuts, big work — but they keep, and fat is fat.
description: a big many-stemmed shrub with round toothed leaves and nuts in ragged leafy cups

knowledgeLevels.1: Hazelnut. A big multi-stemmed shrub; nuts in leafy green cups.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the nut inside the cup and shell. Cup off, crack the shell. The cup's ragged leafy beak means European.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: rich in fat and protein — the forest's butter. Eat fresh or dried; they keep for months.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: coppiced hazel stools fruit heaviest. Float-test (sinkers good). Weevils drill tiny holes — check. Roast lightly to wake the flavor.

lookalikeNote: The leafy cup with a ragged beak is unmistakable. Empty shells mean weevils got there first — float-test your harvest.
name: European Hazelnut
preparation: Husk the leafy cup, dry, crack. Roast briefly to improve flavor.
sources: Plants for a Future (PFAF) — Corylus avellana
Samuel Thayer — Nature's Garden

uses.note: sweet oily nuts — crack carefully, worth the trouble

codex: The oak's old bargain: tons of food, but you have to wash the bitter out first.
description: oval nuts in scaly cups, scattered under the big lobed-leaf trees

knowledgeLevels.1: Acorn. Oak nuts — bitter enough to warn you.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the nutmeat inside the shell. Shell, grind coarse, then leach: soak in several changes of water until the bitterness (tannin) is gone.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: leached acorn meal cooks into porridge or flatbread. A mast year feeds a village — the oaks drop tons.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: taste-test trees — some are far less bitter. Dry before storing or they mold. Leach cold (days) or hot (hours); never skip it.

lookalikeNote: Acorns are acorns — the danger isn't mistaken identity, it's skipping the leach. Bitter means tannin; tannin untreated means misery.
name: Pedunculate Oak Acorn
preparation: Shell, grind, leach tannins in repeated changes of water, then boil or bake. Never eat unleached in quantity.
sources: Plants for a Future (PFAF) — Quercus robur
John Kallas — Edible Wild Plants

uses.note: leached acorn meal — porridge, flatbread

codex: Mast-year gold. The boars know; the jays know. Now you know.
description: tiny three-cornered nuts in spiny husks, under trees with smooth gray bark

knowledgeLevels.1: Beechnut. Small three-sided nuts in spiny little cases under the smooth gray-barked trees.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the triangular nutmeat. A few raw while gathering won't hurt you — but roast before eating in quantity (raw fagin upsets the stomach).
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: rich oily nuts — roast like chestnuts, grind to flour, or press for oil. In mast years the ground is paved with them.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: the spiny cases mostly hold empties — wildlife takes the filled ones first. Roast at a real heat; lukewarm doesn't finish the job.

lookalikeNote: The three-sided nut in a spiny case is unmistakable. The rule isn't identity — it's preparation: roast them.
name: Beechnut
preparation: Shell and ROAST before eating in quantity — raw fagin causes nausea. A taste raw while gathering is harmless.
sources: Plants for a Future (PFAF) — Fagus sylvatica
German Federal Centre for Nutrition (bzfe) — Bucheckern guidance

uses.note: roasted nuts, flour, oil — always heat first

codex: The wild apple. Sour enough to wake the dead, sweet enough after frost to keep you alive.
description: small hard green-yellow apples on a low thorny tree

knowledgeLevels.1: Crab apple. Small hard apples on a thorny little tree.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the whole fruit — eat fresh (tart!), or cook down. The pips have a trace of cyanide compounds; don't make a meal of seeds.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: cook into sauce or roast whole — heat tames the tartness. Dries well for winter.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: after the first frost they're sweeter. Old orchard trees and forest-edge thorn thickets both fruit.

lookalikeNote: Unmistakable once you bite one — nothing else is that tart. Thorny tree + tiny apple = crab apple.
name: Crab Apple
preparation: Eat fresh or cook. Sweeter after frost. Don't chew the pips in quantity.
sources: Plants for a Future (PFAF) — Malus sylvestris
Woodland Trust (UK) — crab apple

uses.note: eat fresh tart, or cook/dry

codex: Summer in a berry. Your fingers will tell the story for days.
description: a low wiry shrub with dusty-blue berries that stain everything purple

knowledgeLevels.1: Bilberry. Low shrub, dusty-blue berries that stain your fingers purple.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the berries — eat fresh by the handful. The stain is the ID: bilberry juice is dark through and through.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the forest's summer sugar. Dries into raisin-like keeps. Leaves make a tea.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: pick with a berry comb in a good year and you'll fill buckets. They fruit best where the pines thin out.

lookalikeNote: Deadly nightshade berries can look like blueberries to a careless picker — but nightshade is a TALL plant with cherry-sized glossy berries in clusters and purple flowers. Bilberry is knee-high, berries single, juice dark. When in doubt, check the plant, not the berry.
name: Bilberry
preparation: Eat fresh or dry. The purple stain on your hands is normal — it's the anthocyanins.
sources: Plants for a Future (PFAF) — Vaccinium myrtillus
Woodland Trust (UK) — bilberry

uses.note: eat fresh, dry for winter

codex: Proof the forest likes you, occasionally.
description: tiny intensely fragrant red berries on low plants along sunny edges

knowledgeLevels.1: Wild strawberry. Tiny red berries, impossibly fragrant.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the berries. Smaller than garden ones, ten times the flavor. The smell gives them away before your eyes do.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: eat fresh — they don't keep and don't need to. A morale crop as much as a food.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: follow your nose along sunny trail edges in June. They hide under their own leaves.

lookalikeNote: Nothing poisonous mimics it closely — the fragrance is the guarantee. Mock strawberry (Potentilla indica) is bland and dry, not dangerous.
name: Woodland Strawberry
preparation: Eat fresh. They bruise if you look at them wrong.
sources: Plants for a Future (PFAF) — Fragaria vesca

uses.note: eat fresh

codex: The hedgerow's pension plan: unglamorous, reliable, everywhere.
description: a thorny small tree with clusters of small red berries

knowledgeLevels.1: Hawthorn. A thorny shrub/small tree with clusters of small red berries.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the haws — mealy, mild, edible raw. Big seed inside; eat around it.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: a steady fall food — not exciting, but everywhere. The old herbals call it a heart tonic (tea from leaves and flowers).
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: best after frost softens them. The thorns are the real harvest hazard — pick with care.

lookalikeNote: Single-seeded red haws on a thorny tree — distinctive. Don't confuse the thorns with blackthorn (sloes are blue-black and mouth-puckering).
name: Hawthorn
preparation: Eat raw around the seed, or cook into a sauce. Leaf/flower tea is the traditional heart tonic.
sources: Plants for a Future (PFAF) — Crataegus monogyna
Woodland Trust (UK) — hawthorn

uses.note: haws raw or cooked
leaf/flower tea — traditional heart tonic

codex: Winter's vitamin C, hanging on a thorn.
description: bright red-orange oval fruits on arching thorny canes

knowledgeLevels.1: Rose hip. Bright red-orange oval fruits on the thorny rose canes.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the fleshy hip around the seeds. Eat the flesh — the seeds inside are covered in itching hairs. Or cook and strain.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: one of the richest wild sources of vitamin C — the scurvy answer when greens are gone. Tea, syrup, or dried.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: harvest after frost when they soften. Dry whole for winter tea; the vitamin C mostly survives drying.

lookalikeNote: Unmistakable on the cane — but never eat the hairy seeds raw; they itch going down and coming out. Strain them.
name: Dog Rose Hip
preparation: Eat the flesh raw avoiding the hairy seeds, or simmer and strain for tea/syrup. Best after frost.
sources: Plants for a Future (PFAF) — Rosa canina
Samuel Thayer — Nature's Garden

uses.note: flesh raw (avoid seeds), tea, syrup
vitamin C — the scurvy answer

codex: June smells of the flowers; September tastes of the syrup. Cook the berries — the bush insists.
description: a big shrub with flat plates of white flowers, later drooping clusters of black berries

knowledgeLevels.1: Elder. Big shrub; flat white flower plates in June, drooping black berry clusters in late summer.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: ripe BLACK berries only — and cook them. Raw berries (and all green parts) can nauseate. The creamy flower heads make a fine tea/fritter cooked.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: cooked berries → syrup, sauce, wine. The classic cold-season remedy — elderberry syrup for winter coughs.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: shake clusters into a bag; strip with a fork. Unripe green/red berries stay on the plant — only the black ones.

lookalikeNote: Ripe black clusters + flat flower-plate memory = elder. Red-berried elders are a different, harsher species — leave red clusters alone.
name: European Elder
preparation: COOK the ripe black berries — raw causes nausea. Flowers: tea or battered and fried.
sources: Plants for a Future (PFAF) — Sambucus nigra
John Kallas — Edible Wild Plants

uses.note: cooked berries — syrup, sauce
elderberry syrup for coughs/colds

codex: Bear's garlic — the bears dig it first. The smell test never lies.
description: broad lily-like leaves carpeting damp spring woods, smelling of garlic

knowledgeLevels.1: Wild garlic. Broad green leaves carpeting damp woods in spring, smelling of garlic.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: leaves (and later the flower buds). The smell test is LAW: crush a leaf — real wild garlic smells strongly of garlic.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the spring tonic green — pesto, soups, wilted like spinach. The bulbs are edible too but leave them; the leaves are the crop.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: harvest leaf-by-leaf, never whole patches. It carpets beech woods in April — where the beech is, the garlic follows.

lookalikeNote: DEADLY confusion possible: lily of the valley and autumn crocus leaves look nearly identical before flowering — but NEITHER smells of garlic. Crush and sniff every handful. No garlic smell = poison. This is the most important ID in the spring woods.
name: Wild Garlic
preparation: Eat raw or wilted/boiled. The garlic smell is the safety check — no smell, no eat.
sources: Plants for a Future (PFAF) — Allium ursinum
Rita Lüder — wild plant guides (DE)

uses.note: leaves raw/wilted — pesto, soup

codex: The king's spinach, outlasting the kings. It grows where people used to live — follow the ruins.
description: spinach-like plants with arrow-shaped dusty-coated leaves near old walls and yards

knowledgeLevels.1: Good King Henry. A spinach-like plant with arrow-shaped dusty leaves, often near old ruins and farmyards.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: young leaves and shoots — cook like spinach. The dusty white coating on young leaves is the ID mark.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the old cottage-garden spinach, gone wild. Boil to tame the oxalic edge; the water goes dark, the greens stay mild.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: perennial — the same plants return yearly. Cut young shoots like asparagus in early spring.

lookalikeNote: The dusty-white mealy coating on young leaves marks it. Older plants resemble orache — still edible, just tougher.
name: Good King Henry
preparation: Boil young leaves/shoots like spinach; discard the water. Eat young — old leaves get harsh.
sources: Plants for a Future (PFAF) — Blitum bonus-henricus
John Kallas — Edible Wild Plants

uses.note: young leaves/shoots boiled like spinach

codex: The forest's lemon. Sour means vitamin C and a warning in the same bite.
description: arrow-shaped leaves with a sharp lemony tang

knowledgeLevels.1: Sorrel. Arrow-shaped leaves with a sharp lemon tang.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the leaves — chew one and the sourness is unmistakable. That tang is oxalic acid: fine as a flavoring, not as a staple.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: soup green (the classic sorrel soup), salad accent. A little goes a long way.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: the arrowhead leaf with pointed basal lobes is the mark. Don't live on it — oxalic acid in bulk is hard on kidneys.

lookalikeNote: The lemon tang is the ID — nothing sour-tasting and arrow-leaved in these meadows will hurt you in normal amounts.
name: Common Sorrel
preparation: Eat sparingly raw; cook into soups. A flavoring green, not a bulk green.
sources: Plants for a Future (PFAF) — Rumex acetosa

uses.note: leaves raw sparingly, soup green

codex: The Romans planted it as food and it never left. Neither should you, in April.
description: creeping patches of divided toothed leaves in shady damp spots

knowledgeLevels.1: Ground elder. Creeping patches of divided leaves in shady spots.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: young spring leaves — the Romans ate it as a potherb. Older leaves get harsh; take the young unfolded ones.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: cook like spinach. Abundant enough to be a real bulk green in April and May.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: the leaflets in threes with toothed edges, on grooved stems. It was a gout remedy once — hence podagraria.

lookalikeNote: Young leaves are safe and distinctive in threes. As with all umbel-family lookers, check the stem: ground elder stems are grooved, not purple-spotted (hemlock's mark).
name: Ground Elder
preparation: Boil young leaves like spinach. Take young unfolded leaves; old ones are harsh.
sources: Plants for a Future (PFAF) — Aegopodium podagraria

uses.note: young leaves boiled like spinach

codex: The carrot's wild grandmother. The smell test is the difference between dinner and a funeral.
description: lacy white flower heads on tall stems; thin pale roots

knowledgeLevels.1: Wild carrot. Lacy white flower umbels; thin white roots.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: first-year roots (before it flowers). Scrape a root — real wild carrot smells of carrot. No carrot smell = don't dig.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: thin but real roots — soup material. The seeds are a sharp spice.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: first-year rosette only; second-year roots go woody. And the deadly rule: hemlock grows beside it — carrot smell or walk away.

lookalikeNote: POISON HEMLOCK is the deadly twin: hemlock has smooth purple-spotted stems and a foul mousy smell; wild carrot has hairy green stems and smells of carrot. Smell the root. When in doubt, walk away — hemlock kills.
name: Wild Carrot
preparation: Scrub and boil first-year roots. Confirm the carrot smell before eating.
sources: Samuel Thayer — Nature's Garden
Plants for a Future (PFAF) — Daucus carota

uses.note: first-year roots boiled — confirm carrot smell

codex: May's lace. Beautiful, edible — and the reason you learn hemlock before you learn lunch.
description: frothy white flower umbels on tall ridged stems along hedgerows

knowledgeLevels.1: Cow parsley. Frothy white umbels along every hedgerow in May.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: young leaves and shoots — mild, parsley-like. But this family demands respect: learn hemlock's marks first.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: a spring salad leaf in small amounts. Never the default green — the risk/reward only works when you're certain.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: ridged, slightly hairy green stems, NO purple spots, fresh green smell. Hemlock: smooth stem, purple spots, mousy stink. Know both cold.

lookalikeNote: Hemlock again: purple-spotted smooth stems + foul smell = death. Cow parsley: ridged hairy green stems, no spots, fresh smell. If you can't tell them apart yet, don't pick either.
name: Cow Parsley
preparation: Young leaves raw in small amounts or wilted. Only when hemlock's marks are memorized.
sources: Plants for a Future (PFAF) — Anthriscus sylvestris
Woodland Trust (UK) — cow parsley

uses.note: young leaves — only with hemlock ID certain

codex: Gold in the moss. The apricot smell is the signature — learn it once, eat for life.
description: golden funnel-shaped mushrooms with an apricot smell, in mossy woods

knowledgeLevels.1: Chanterelle. Golden funnel-shaped mushrooms smelling faintly of apricots.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the whole mushroom — but ALWAYS cook wild mushrooms. The false chanterelle has true thin gills; real chanterelles have blunt forked ridges, not gills.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the prized one — sauté in fat. They fruit in the same mossy spots year after year; remember the spot.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: ridges not gills, apricot smell, flesh white inside. Cut, don't pull — the mycelium fruits again.

lookalikeNote: False chanterelle (Hygrophoropsis aurantiaca): true thin gills, darker orange, no apricot smell — not deadly but a bad meal. Real ones have blunt ridges, not gills.
name: Chanterelle
preparation: ALWAYS cook wild mushrooms. Sauté; never eat raw.
sources: Roger Phillips — Mushrooms (Collins Complete Guide)
Rita Lüder — Grundkurs Pilzbestimmung

uses.note: sautéed — always cooked

codex: Steinpilz. The mushroom that built foraging cultures — dry them and winter gets easier.
description: big brown-capped mushrooms with thick pale stems and sponge pores, no gills

knowledgeLevels.1: Porcini. Big brown-capped boletes with thick pale stems, under spruce and beech.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: cap and stem — cook always. Check the pores: white-to-olive sponge, no gills. Nibble-and-spit a crumb: bitter = the inedible bitter bolete.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: the king of mushrooms — fresh sautéed or dried (they dry superbly and keep all winter).
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: white net-like pattern on the upper stem marks true porcini. Slice stems lengthwise — maggots show as tunnels; share with no one.

lookalikeNote: Bitter bolete (Tylopilus felleus) looks alike but isn't poisonous — just vile. Nibble and spit: bitter = toss it. No gilled mushroom is a bolete.
name: Porcini
preparation: ALWAYS cook. Dry surplus — dried porcini are winter gold.
sources: Roger Phillips — Mushrooms (Collins Complete Guide)
Rita Lüder — Grundkurs Pilzbestimmung

uses.note: sautéed fresh or dried — always cooked

codex: A soccer ball you can eat — if it's white all the way through. The cut test is non-negotiable.
description: a huge smooth white ball sitting on the ground, sometimes head-sized

knowledgeLevels.1: Giant puffball. A huge white ball on the ground — sometimes the size of your head.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the whole ball, sliced like bread and fried — BUT only if pure white inside. Cut top to bottom: any hint of a cap-and-stem shape inside means a deadly Amanita button. Walk away.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: mild, filling — fry slices like tofu steaks. One ball feeds several people.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: pure white and marshmallow-firm = good. Any yellowing = too old (stomach trouble). Small round whites are the dangerous ones to confuse — only take the giants you're sure of.

lookalikeNote: Young death caps and destroying angels look like small white balls before they open. The rule: cut top to bottom — pure white and featureless throughout, or it isn't food. Any shadow of gills, cap, or stem = deadly.
name: Giant Puffball
preparation: Slice and fry. ONLY when uniformly pure white inside — cut every specimen top to bottom first.
sources: Roger Phillips — Mushrooms (Collins Complete Guide)
Missouri Dept. of Conservation — giant puffball field guide

uses.note: fried slices — only pure-white specimens

codex: Beautiful, fragrant, lethal. The reason the smell test exists.
description: broad paired leaves with sweet white bell flowers in spring, red berries later

knowledgeLevels.1: Lily of the valley. Sweet white bell flowers in spring; broad leaves otherwise.
knowledgeLevels.2: POISON. Cardiac glycosides — every part, especially the red berries. The leaves are the wild-garlic killer: identical-looking, no garlic smell.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: none as food. Know it so you don't eat it by mistake.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: two broad leaves per stem, no garlic smell when crushed. Teach everyone the smell test.

lookalikeNote: The wild-garlic twin that kills: same broad leaves, same woods, same season — but crush it and there's NO garlic smell. Smell every leaf.
name: Lily of the Valley
preparation: DO NOT EAT. All parts toxic.
sources: Plants for a Future (PFAF) — Convallaria majalis

codex: It flowers without leaves and leafs without flowers — and punishes the careless in both seasons.
description: broad fleshy leaves in spring (no flowers), purple crocus flowers in fall (no leaves)

knowledgeLevels.1: Autumn crocus. Purple crocus-like flowers in fall with NO leaves; broad leaves in spring with no flowers.
knowledgeLevels.2: POISON. Colchicine — a few grams can kill. The spring leaves are the second wild-garlic killer: broad, green, garlic-smell-free.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: none as food. A medicine plant for specialists only — not you, not now.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: leaves emerge from a bulb-like corm with no stem; wild garlic leaves have distinct stems. When in doubt, smell.

lookalikeNote: Meadow saffron's spring leaves mimic wild garlic — thicker, fleshier, stemless, and smelling of nothing. The garlic smell test catches it.
name: Autumn Crocus
preparation: DO NOT EAT. Colchicine poisoning is slow and irreversible.
sources: Plants for a Future (PFAF) — Colchicum autumnale

codex: The one that ends foragers. Half a cap, no second chances. Respect is survival.
description: an olive-green capped mushroom with white gills, a skirt-like ring, and a sac at the stem base

knowledgeLevels.1: Death cap. An olive-green capped mushroom with white gills, a ring on the stem, and a cup at the base.
knowledgeLevels.2: POISON. Amatoxins — half a cap can kill an adult. It tastes fine; that's the horror. The young 'buttons' look like small white balls.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: none. Learn it to avoid it — and to warn others.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: greenish cap + white gills + stem ring + basal cup (volva) = walk away. Dig up the base to check for the cup; the cup is the signature.

lookalikeNote: Kills more foragers than any other mushroom. Buttons mimic puffballs and field mushrooms — always excavate the base: the volva sac gives it away.
name: Death Cap
preparation: DO NOT EAT. There is no safe preparation.
sources: Roger Phillips — Mushrooms (Collins Complete Guide)
Rita Lüder — Grundkurs Pilzbestimmung

codex: The mushroom every child draws and no forager eats.
description: the classic red-and-white-spotted toadstool

knowledgeLevels.1: Fly agaric. The storybook mushroom — bright red cap with white warts.
knowledgeLevels.2: POISON. Ibotenic acid — toxic and deliriant, not usually deadly but never food. The white warts wash off in rain, so don't trust a 'plain red' ID.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: none as food. The fairy-tale look is the warning — nature's red flag.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: same family as the death cap — white gills, stem ring, basal cup. If it has the amanita architecture, it isn't dinner.

lookalikeNote: Unmistakable when fresh — but rain washes the white warts off, leaving a plain red cap. Check the stem base for the amanita cup regardless.
name: Fly Agaric
preparation: DO NOT EAT. Toxic and psychoactive — not food by any preparation you should attempt.
sources: Roger Phillips — Mushrooms (Collins Complete Guide)

codex: Belladonna — the beautiful lady with a body count. Sweet berries, bitter end.
description: a tall plant with dull purple bell flowers and shiny black cherry-sized berries

knowledgeLevels.1: Deadly nightshade. A tall plant with purple bell flowers and shiny black cherry-like berries.
knowledgeLevels.2: POISON. Atropine — a few berries can kill. Sweet-tasting, which is why children die of it.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: none as food. The berries can look like big bilberries to the careless — check the plant: nightshade is waist-high with purple bells.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: solitary shiny berries in leaf axils, purple-brown bells. Teach children on sight — this one kills the young first.

lookalikeNote: The bilberry confusion kills: nightshade berries are cherry-sized, glossy, on a TALL plant with purple bell flowers. Bilberries are pea-sized on a knee-high shrub. Size and height tell them apart.
name: Deadly Nightshade
preparation: DO NOT EAT. A few berries are a lethal dose.
sources: Plants for a Future (PFAF) — Atropa belladonna

codex: What killed Socrates grows by the creek. Purple spots, smooth stem — learn it like your life depends on it.
description: tall white flower umbels on smooth purple-blotched stems, smelling faintly foul

knowledgeLevels.1: Poison hemlock. Tall white umbels on smooth stems blotched purple.
knowledgeLevels.2: POISON. Coniine — Socrates' cup. Every part kills; the roots are the worst. The purple-spotted smooth stem is the mark.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: none. Learn it because everything you want to eat has a cousin that looks like this.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: smooth hollow stem + purple blotches + foul mousy smell when crushed = hemlock, always. Wild carrot: hairy green stem, carrot smell. Cow parsley: ridged hairy stem, no spots.

lookalikeNote: The killer all edible umbels are measured against. Purple spots + smooth stem + mousy stink = death. Memorize it before you pick a single wild carrot.
name: Poison Hemlock
preparation: DO NOT EAT. No safe part, no safe preparation.
sources: Plants for a Future (PFAF) — Conium maculatum
Samuel Thayer — Nature's Garden

codex: The forest's spring water — sweet, free, and gone by May. Take little, thank the tree.
description: white-barked birch trunks weeping sweet sap in early spring

knowledgeLevels.1: Birch sap. In early spring the white-barked birches run sweet — tap a trunk and it weeps.
knowledgeLevels.2: Parts: the spring sap — a thin sweet drink, faintly mineral. Tap high-side, small hole, and never take much from one tree.
knowledgeLevels.3: Uses: drink fresh as a spring tonic; boil down to syrup (it takes a LOT of sap). The year's first sweet thing.
knowledgeLevels.4: Mastery: tap when nights freeze and days thaw — the run lasts weeks. Plug the hole with a twig after; the tree gave you a gift, don't wound it.

lookalikeNote: White peeling bark + drooping twigs = silver birch. Tap birches, not beeches — and only in the spring run.
name: Birch Sap
preparation: Drink fresh or boil to syrup. Tap modestly; plug the tap hole.
sources: Plants for a Future (PFAF) — Betula pendula
Woodland Trust (UK) — silver birch

uses.note: drink fresh, boil to syrup
